passage: Rehana, twenty, needed a laptop for her design course in Lucknow before term began. On Monday she opened three review sites. By Wednesday she had forty tabs, two comparison spreadsheets and a forum thread where strangers argued about screen colours. Every laptop had someone saying it was terrible. At night she lay awake thinking, what if I pick wrong and regret it for four years? Her friend Sahil found her on Friday, staring at the same two models. "Which one did you like on Monday?" "The grey one." "And now?" "I don't know anymore. I know too much." Sahil closed the laptop lid. "What do you actually need it to do?" She listed three things. The grey one did all three.

qa.q: How many tabs did Rehana have open by Wednesday?
qa.a: She had forty tabs.

qa.q: What was Rehana afraid of as she lay awake?
qa.a: She was afraid of picking wrong and regretting it for four years, which made her keep reading and feel more confused.

qa.q: What helped Rehana finally decide?
qa.a: Sahil's question about what she actually needed brought her back to three requirements, which the grey laptop met.

qa.q: How might Sahil see the forty tabs?
qa.a: Sahil seems to see them as making things worse, and closes the laptop to bring the focus back to her real needs.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading endless reviews and becoming more confused, with fear of regret feeding the research.

Sachin: "Dilnaz, you still haven't joined a coaching centre for the entrance exam?"
Dilnaz: "I've been researching. There are six in the city. I've read every review."
Sachin: "And?"
Dilnaz: "One has great results but a rude teacher. One is cheap but crowded. One has good notes but someone said the mock tests are too easy. Another forum says the opposite."
Sachin: "How long have you been reading?"
Dilnaz: "Three weeks."
Sachin: "Classes started two weeks ago."
Dilnaz: "I know! But what if I pick the wrong one and waste the whole year?"
Sachin: "Pick the two nearest your home. Go to a free demo class at each this week. Decide on Sunday."
Dilnaz: "Just two? And no more reviews?"
Sachin: "No more reviews."

qa.q: How many coaching centres were in the city?
qa.a: There are six in the city.

qa.a: Dilnaz felt anxious and confused, afraid of picking the wrong one and wasting the whole year.

passage: I'm Dhruv, and last year I spent a month choosing a paying-guest room in Bengaluru. I visited five, read every online review, joined two groups where people complained about water supply and landlords. Each new comment made me doubt the room I'd liked. One day I'd want the one near college; the next I'd read about its noisy road and panic. My friend Jomon finally asked, "Are you choosing a room or a life partner?" I laughed, but it stung. The best rooms got taken while I read. In the end I took one of the last left, and it was fine. More reading hadn't made me surer. It had just made me scared.

Dear Jahnavi,

You asked how I chose between the two internships. Honestly, I didn't know enough to be sure, so I stopped trying to be sure.

I wrote down what I didn't know: whether the Mumbai one would give real work, whether I could afford rent there, and whether the Delhi one would lead to a job. Then I found cheap ways to learn: I messaged two past interns on each, and asked my cousin about rent.

I gave myself till Friday. My default was Delhi, because I could live at home. The past interns said Mumbai gave real projects, but rent was too high. So Delhi it was. If something changes, I'll rethink.

Pooja

Two offers. Kochi: a stable bank job, near Amma, decent pay. Bengaluru: a start-up, more exciting, but no one knows if it will survive the year. Both want an answer by Thursday.

Thomas

Career counsellor's note, Thursday.
Reena, twenty-five, came in today visibly tired. She has an offer to move to Singapore for work. She described a family meeting last weekend: her father fears she will not return, her aunt Nirmala insists that moving abroad is the only way to grow, and her grandmother fears for her marriage prospects. Each spoke firmly. Reena said, "I respect all of them. But it's like they're deciding their own lives through me." I suggested she write down her own reasons first, then share them with each relative separately, listening to their fears without agreeing to decide by them. She plans to talk to her father on Sunday. We meet again next week.

Dear Diary, Sunday
Told the family I'm thinking of leaving the bank job to become a physiotherapist. Mummy (Sudha) went pale and said I'd be throwing away security. Mama said physiotherapy doesn't pay. Chachi said I should first get married. My cousin said follow my passion. Everyone was so sure.
I didn't argue. I just listened, and wrote down each worry. Some were useful: money, how long the course takes. Some were just their fears.
I'm not deciding tonight. I'll speak to two physiotherapists this week and check the course fees. It's my life, and I still love them for caring. 🤍
Ojas

Wednesday. The lassi sold well. Then her regional head offered her a transfer to a new branch in another city, a two-year commitment. This time she didn't answer on the spot. She asked for a week.
Saturday. She had visited the new branch, called two managers who'd worked there, and talked to her parents. Lokesh said, "You chose the lassi in five minutes and this in six days?" She smiled. "One of them I can undo."

The cycle, I sold within a year. Both choices were right.

Class teacher's note, Class 4, after the safety drill.
Today we practised what to do in an emergency at home. Each child had to say the emergency number, their full address and the name and number of a trusted adult. Akash knew all three instantly; he told us his family practises at dinner. Chinmay knew the number but stumbled on his address and did not know any adult's phone number by heart. He looked embarrassed. I reassured him that this is exactly why we practise. I have sent a note home asking families to help each child learn their address and one adult's number. We will repeat the drill in two weeks.

During the 800-metre race, a runner from another school collapsed near the stands. Within seconds, about thirty students crowded around. I saw Uday, one of our Class 10 boys, standing at the front with his phone in his hand, looking at the runner. Nobody was calling. Later he told me, "I thought someone must have already called." I pushed through, knelt by the runner and pointed at him: "Uday, you. Call 108 now. Tell them the school ground on Ring Road." He dialled at once. I asked Manjula ma'am to clear the crowd. The ambulance came in twelve minutes. On Monday I will talk to the class about why naming one person matters.

passage:
Dear Diary, Tuesday.
Something happened near the bus stop today that I keep thinking about. An old man on a scooter skidded and fell. People gathered, maybe twenty of us. Everyone was looking. I thought, someone has surely called the ambulance already. I didn't move.
Then Sharmila didi, who works at the pharmacy, came out and pointed straight at me. "You. Call 108. Tell them outside the Shiv Mandir bus stop." My hands shook but I did it. She sent two other boys to stop the traffic. The ambulance came.
Afterwards I realised: nobody had called. Everyone thought someone else had. That could have been Dadaji.
Omkar

subtype: Basic first aid course and calm hands [Actor]
passage: In the college hostel common room, Joseph cut his palm on a broken glass while washing up. Blood ran down his wrist. People shouted. Alka, twenty, who had done a first-aid course last term, felt her heart jump, then her training kicked in. She checked for more glass on the floor, moved people back and said, "Someone call the warden and the ambulance, now." She took a clean towel, pressed it firmly on the cut and asked Joseph to hold his hand up. She didn't try to pull anything out of the wound or clean it; that wasn't what she'd been taught to do. She kept talking to him calmly until the warden arrived with the nurse.

qa.a: He cut his palm on a broken glass while washing up.

qa.a: She felt her heart jump with alarm, then steadied as her training took over.

qa.a: She checked for danger, called for the warden and ambulance, and pressed a towel on the cut; she didn't pull anything from the wound because that was beyond her training.

qa.a: Joseph likely felt frightened but calmer and safer, hearing her steady voice until help arrived.

subtype: Basic first aid course and calm hands [Actor]
passage:
Dear Karthik,

You asked if the first-aid course was worth it. Let me tell you what happened on Saturday.

At the bus stand, a woman tripped on the kerb and cut her forehead. There was a lot of blood and people just stared. I was scared, honestly. But I remembered the steps. I checked that no bus was coming. I asked a shopkeeper to call 108. I pressed my clean handkerchief on the cut and asked her to sit down. That's all. I didn't try to do more than we'd been taught.

The ambulance came in fifteen minutes. The paramedic said the pressure helped.

So yes, do the course.

Yamini

qa.a: The ambulance came in fifteen minutes.

qa.a: Yamini felt scared, but the practised steps brought steadiness.

passage: On a rainy night in Chennai, Mohit, nineteen, and his friend Amandeep were walking home when a scooter skidded ahead of them. The rider lay on the road, groaning, one leg bent oddly. Mohit had never done first aid. His legs felt like water. But he stepped into the road and waved his phone torch at the traffic while Amandeep dialled 112. "Don't lift him," the operator said. "Is he breathing? Keep him still and talk to him." Mohit knelt beside the rider and kept him from trying to sit up. "Help is coming. What's your name?" He repeated the operator's questions aloud to Amandeep. The ambulance came. Mohit's hands shook for an hour afterwards.

qa.q: What did Mohit use to warn the traffic?
qa.a: He waved his phone torch at the traffic.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when he saw the rider on the road?
qa.a: He felt terrified, his legs like water, since he had never done first aid.

qa.q: What did Mohit and Amandeep do right, even without training?
qa.a: They made the scene safe, called 112, followed the operator's instructions, kept the rider still and stayed with him until the ambulance came.

qa.a: The rider, in pain and frightened, likely felt a little calmer with someone beside him saying help was coming.

passage: I'm Swati, and I've never done a first-aid course. But last month, at the college gate, my classmate Reena fainted and hit her head on the pavement. People crowded close.
